excerpt:
The unit of account in this book is the work, not the agent. A work unit is a
case file: who authorized it, what it may touch, what it did, what evidence it
left, what it still owes, and who pays if it fails. Every chapter builds or
defends one part of that file. The chapters are ordered so that each stands on
the ones before it, and each proving chapter follows the chapter whose promises
it discharges. Read in order for the argument, or enter at the question you
need: where a rule can be made real (\pdchapref{swk}{The Single-Writer
Kernel}); how authority travels without growing (\pdchapref{anchor}{The Anchor
Protocol}); what two owners who distrust each other may compute together,
and what its only exit may leak (\pdchapref{sealed}{The Sealed Harbor});
what an operator must be able to see (\pdchapref{ls}{The Legible
Swarm}); what remains long enough to owe anything (\pdchapref{stp}{From Spawn
to Person}); what makes exchange rational (\pdchapref{he}{The Harbor Economy});
who may decide, on what evidence (\pdchapref{bonded}{The Bonded Commons}); and
what may cross a trust boundary (\pdchapref{fh}{The Federated Harbor}). No
chapter carries its own abstract or reader's map, in this edition or any
other; each chapter simply opens on the question it answers and begins with
its argument. What follows is the one reader's map this book keeps: not a
table repeated once per chapter, but a single figure tracing five kinds of
reader through the book's four parts, drawn once, in front, where a route can
be checked against the whole argument instead of guessed one chapter at a
time.
explanation: Replace duplicated eight-chapter inventory and production commentary with task-led entry routes, prerequisites and stop conditions.
rewrite:
A work unit records who authorized a job, what it may touch, what happened,
and who remains responsible afterward. The chapters develop the mechanisms
needed to keep that record useful across concurrent work, restarts, and
transactions between operators.

Read chapters 1--8 in order for the full argument. For a first visit, choose
a question below. These are short entry routes; the facing-page map shows
where to continue for a deeper reading.

\begin{description}[style=nextline,leftmargin=0pt]
\item[Why do agents need coordination?]
Start with Mara's refactor in \hyperref[ls:sec:mara]{Chapter 4's worked
afternoon}. Follow the failure taxonomy and the summary-with-evidence
example. Stop when you can explain why a green test report may still need
inspection. You do not need the information-theory derivation on this pass.
\item[What survives a crash?]
Read \hyperref[swk:sec:durability]{Chapter 1's durability section} and its
fault-class table, then the recovery discussion. Check that you can
distinguish a process crash from power loss before following the proofs.
\item[What may a delegated agent do?]
Start with \hyperref[anchor:sec:problem]{Chapter 2's reused-process-ID
example}, then follow the permission chain and its limitations. Continue
to Chapter 3 if your question concerns data confinement.
\item[How could two operators trade work?]
Read Chapter 5's restart example, then Chapter 6's worked settlement.
Use Chapters 7 and 8 to inspect disputes and cross-machine assumptions.
An ability to follow the ledger arithmetic is enough for the first pass.
\end{description}

\noindent This is a book about mechanisms and their limits, not an installation

the \hyperref[app:volume-status]{implementation boundary} and check the
current software separately. The chapter's label tells you what kind of

excerpt: Two autonomous coding agents share a repository. Agent~A is asked to refactor the authentication middleware. Agent~B, spawned ninety seconds later from a sibling worktree, is asked to add a rate-limiter to the same middleware. Neither knows the other exists. They both edit, both commit, both push; one of them gets a merge conflict it cannot interpret, retries with a hallucinated resolution, and corrupts the file. The operator returns from a coffee break to a working tree she does not recognize. This is not a hypothetical---it is the modal failure mode of every multi-agent setup we have inhabited. Existing frameworks do not address it: LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen handle state graphs and role assignment competently; the Model Context Protocol standardizes agent-tool integration. None of them give Agent~A and Agent~B a way to know about each other. The problem is \textbf{trust}---specifically, trust as infrastructure rather than trust as per-transaction ceremony.
explanation: Remove unsupported modal-failure frequency and blanket competitor dismissal.
rewrite:
Consider two coding agents working on the same authentication middleware.
Agent~A refactors it; Agent~B starts ninety seconds later in a sibling
worktree and adds a rate-limiter. Neither knows about the other's task.
When their changes conflict, one agent accepts an incorrect merge resolution.
The operator returns to a broken file and must reconstruct who changed what.

Scheduling tasks and connecting tools do not by themselves settle this
dispute. The operator also needs a record of authority, actions, and outcomes,
plus a rule for assigning responsibility. This chapter develops that shared
institution.

excerpt: The standard response in security engineering is ``zero trust''---never trust, always verify. But zero trust applied literally to agent coordination is paralytic. If every message requires cryptographic verification, every delegation requires capability negotiation, and every file access requires authorization---the coordination overhead overwhelms the work itself. Agents spend their context windows negotiating trust instead of solving problems.
explanation: Distinguish negotiation costs from verification; remove caricature of zero trust.
rewrite:
Repeated negotiation can consume agent time and context. The design here
moves common admission rules into the commons authority while retaining
verification at the relevant boundaries. It does not require abandoning
per-message authentication or access checks.
line_basis: Post-edit source line of the exact rewrite, checked 2026-09-18.

excerpt: This chapter argues that multi-agent systems need exactly this: a \textbf{commons authority} that provides trust as infrastructure, not trust as ceremony. Agents don't negotiate trust per-transaction. They enter a commons where trust has already been established---structurally, evidentially, and economically---and they work freely within that trust envelope.
explanation: Replace blanket trust claim with conditional mechanism.
rewrite:
A \textbf{commons authority} supplies shared admission, attribution, and
settlement rules. Agents enter under those rules, but admission alone does
not establish good behavior. The incentive and monitoring assumptions below
determine which risks the arrangement can limit.
line_basis: Post-edit source line of the exact rewrite, checked 2026-09-18.

excerpt: A demonstration is scheduled for 4pm. Alice runs the back end of the demo on her laptop; Bob runs the front end on his. Each has a working Port Daddy daemon: capability tokens are minted and attenuated under the Anchor Protocol~\pdcite{owens2026anchor}, the workspace history is Merkle-chained and replicated locally per the Bonded Commons~\pdcite{owens2026bonded}, and bonds for cleanup of botched migrations are posted in the local collateral pool. Inside each laptop, the trust story is closed and the formal-verification artifacts hold.

excerpt: This chapter extends the Anchor Protocol, the Bonded Commons, and the daemon-as-correlation-device argument to the multi-administrative-domain case. We are not introducing a new substrate; we are showing that the existing substrate admits a clean federation, and that the federation rules are sharper than they look. Where the prior papers spoke of \emph{the} commons authority, this chapter speaks of a \emph{mesh of} mutually witnessing commons authorities, each sovereign inside its own machine, none sovereign over the others, and all of them bound to the same audit substrate.
explanation: Remove self-assessed sharpness and proven-composition implication.
rewrite:
This chapter proposes a federation of commons authorities, using the
Anchor Protocol and Bonded Commons as local components. Each authority
governs its own machine and witnesses records from its peers. The protocols
below specify how they exchange evidence without granting one authority
control over another.

excerpt: The two-machine problem is the structural sequel to the local-swarm problem of Anchor and the trust-as-infrastructure argument of Bonded. The proposed answer is not a new substrate but a clean extension: keep each daemon sovereign inside its own machine, add a shared witness log that no harbor controls, hang revocation gossip and conditionally restricted custody off the witness log, and gate federation admission on bonded sponsorship rather than permissionless entry. Each primitive does exactly one job. Each primitive is honest about what it does not do.
explanation: Shorten repetitive conclusion; remove personified honesty.
rewrite:
The proposed federation keeps local authority with each daemon. A shared
witness log supports revocation records and conditionally restricted custody;
bonded sponsorship controls admission. These mechanisms require the
implementation and service-level assumptions stated in the chapter.
